You have been standing here for almost ten minutes. Most people give this one about thirty seconds.
I know. I came for the big canvases in the next room, but this one is strangely arresting.
Strangely how? Tell me what is holding you here.
The light, mostly. The whole corner is suffused with it, but it does not feel dramatic. It feels like an ordinary Tuesday morning.
That is a good way of putting it. I usually tell groups to find the one thing in the picture that moves.
The milk. It is the only thing in motion, and she treats it as if spilling a single drop would be a disaster.
When I was your age, I thought this was the most boring picture in the whole museum. It took me years, and a very patient professor, to see it.
She made us write two pages about it without using the word beautiful. I was furious with her for a week. Then I started actually looking.
That sounds exactly like the kind of prompt I am going to find on every college application.

Welcome to stop fourteen, the smallest painting in this gallery and, for many visitors, the one they remember longest. Johannes Vermeer painted The Milkmaid around 1658, when he was still in his twenties and still working out what kind of painter he wanted to be. Before you read anything else, take a moment simply to look. Notice where the light comes from. It enters through the window on the left and settles on the woman's face, on her arms and on the bread on the table. Now step a little closer and look at the crust of that bread. Those tiny raised dots are not an accident. Vermeer placed them one by one, so that the surface would seem to glitter. The blue of her apron was made from one of the most expensive pigments a painter could buy, which tells you how seriously he took this humble scene. Finally, look at the wall behind her. It is almost empty. Vermeer chose to leave it that way, and that emptiness is doing more work than any decoration could. When you are ready, please continue to stop fifteen.

Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Introduction to Art History. Before we look at a single slide this semester, I want to tell you what this course will actually ask of you, because it is not what most of you expect. You probably think the hard part is memorizing names and dates. It is not. The hard part is describing what you see so precisely that someone who has never seen the work could imagine it. That practice has an old name, ekphrasis, and it is the foundation of everything we will do together. Your first assignment is due next Thursday. Choose one painting in the university museum, stand in front of it for at least twenty minutes, and then write six hundred words about it. There are two rules. You may not use the words beautiful, amazing or interesting, and you may not look anything up before you write. I want your eyes, not the internet's. Most of you will find the first ten minutes unbearably slow. Stay anyway. That is exactly the moment when you start to see.
